translation:
M. Tsanyo

The Holy Community of Łuków

The ancient community of Łuków was situated, geographically and strategically, at a bustling crossroads between Poland and Lithuania, and dominated the plain of Podlasie. Perhaps that is why Łuków was the oldest Jewish settlement in Podlasie. Before the Christians built a church, the Jews had already built their own synagogue there. If the city did not witness the tumultuous campaigns of Khmelnytsky’s bands, the Swedes, Napoleon’s army, the Russians, and others, this was only because those passing through plundered, murdered, and burned everything so thoroughly that nothing remained for those who came afterward. As turbulent as the history of the royal city was, so turbulent and full of life were the lives of Łuków’s Jews. The holy community of Łuków had great lineage; it had Podlasie’s important rabbis, and its last rabbi, if I am not mistaken, was a grandson of the Kotzker.

Just as the flame of Kotzk Hasidism burned in all its colors, so later, until the Holocaust, burned the flame of Hasidism for a national vision and social liberation—at least for the entire world. The Jews of Łuków were of the Podlasie stock: healthy, hardworking, honest, and not a little conservative. In the struggle between the Mitnagdim and the Hasidim, the Jews of Łuków fought against Hasidism like lions; but once they had tasted Hasidism, not even one Mitnaged remained in Łuków—there was no remedy. Likewise, in modern times the Jews of Łuków knew no compromises—immersed in everything: immersed in Zionism, immersed in Bundism; and if revolution, then a worldwide one, such as would not leave even the most distant village somewhere in Asia untouched...
translatorNotes: “ק״ק לוקוב” is rendered as “The Holy Community of Łuków,” a conventional translation of the Hebrew abbreviation for a Jewish community.
“המשור של פודלישה” appears to mean “the plain of Podlasie”; the OCR wording is somewhat uncertain.
“הקוצקאי” refers to the Kotzker, i.e., the Hasidic rabbi associated with Kotzk.
“לא נמצא בלוקוב אפילו מתנגד לרפואה” is translated closely as “not even one Mitnaged remained in Łuków—there was no remedy”; the Hebrew phrase is idiomatic and possibly OCR-uncertain.
